162.title: Aad sach: the meaning
162.hook: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and true hereafter, says Nanak
162.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the salok on the eternal truth every morning after the Mool Mantar, and sach, the True, is a name for God found all through the Guru Granth Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound: aad sach, jugaad sach, hai bhee sach, Naanak hosee bhee sach. Your line was let the last sach fade.

We use the word true in two ways. A true statement happens to be so: it's raining, it's Tuesday. That kind of true can change by tomorrow. A true friend is the one who stays, who still shows up after the move, the divorce, the bad year. That kind of true is about lasting. Guru Nanak's salok uses the second kind. Yesterday you heard it; today, what it says.
screen: `TRUE: IT HAPPENS TO BE SO.` → `TRUE: IT STAYS.` → `TODAY, THE MEANING.`

segments.voice: Sach is truth, the true. In Gurbani it's more than a correct fact. It's a name for the One: the reality that doesn't wear out. The Mool Mantar said it first: sat naam, truth is the name. Now the salok spells it out in four steps. Following Macauliffe, in plain words: true in the beginning, true through the ages, true even now, and, says Nanak, true it shall be hereafter. Aad: the beginning, before anything was. Jugaad: through the ages, the long cycles of time Indian thought counts in. Hai bhee: is, even now, at this moment. Hosee bhee: will be, ever after. Listen for the small word bhee: also, even. True then, and also now. True now, and also later. The passing of time takes nothing away. Notice what isn't there: no argument, no proof. Guru Nanak doesn't reason his way to it; he states it, the way you'd name a mountain you can see. Japji will spend thirty-eight pauris on how a person comes to live inside that truth. And notice the name in the middle: Nanak. The Guru signs his hymns with it, and the later Gurus in the Granth sign theirs as Nanak too. It's a signature, and a witness: this is what Nanak saw. Why begin here? Because everything that follows, a restless mind, a changing world, fame and loss, stands in front of something that doesn't change. That's the ground Japji is built on.
screen: `SACH — THE TRUE THAT LASTS.` · `BEGINNING, AGES, NOW, HEREAFTER.` · `BHEE — ALSO, EVEN NOW.` · `NANAK SIGNS AS WITNESS.` · then, large: `SACH.`

segments.voice: Picture yourself at seven, at fifteen, a year ago, and now: your face, your work, your opinions, your address have all changed. Look for one thing that hasn't, maybe a way you love people, a stubborn honesty, a sense of wonder, a fear you've always faced anyway, and name it quietly to yourself: true then, and true now. If you pray, you can hold it up to the One the salok calls true.
Sach. Truth, the true that lasts: true in the beginning, through the ages, now, and hereafter.
Your line: true then, true now. Four times named, and nothing taken away. See you tomorrow.

163.title: Pauri 1, sound: sochai soch
163.hook: sochai soch na hovaee je sochee lakh vaar
163.tomorrow: Pauri 1, meaning: the wall of falsehood
163.howItsDone: The first pauri of Japji is recited each morning right after the opening salok; many Sikhs know it by heart from hearing it daily.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sach: true in the beginning, through the ages, now and hereafter. Your line was true then, true now.

Two in the morning, lying awake, going over the same conversation for the fortieth time. Planning what you'll say. Rehearsing. Turning it over, as if one more lap will settle it. Ever tried to solve a feeling by thinking about it? The first real verse of Japji starts right there, inside the thinking. And it opens with an almost tongue-twister: the same word twice in a row, like a person pacing a room.
screen: `TWO IN THE MORNING.` → `THE SAME CONVERSATION, AGAIN.` → `A LINE THAT PACES.`

segments.voice: A pauri is a step, a rung on a ladder. Japji is built from thirty-eight of them, and this is the first. Its opening line: sochai soch na hovaee, je sochee lakh vaar. Sound it out. Sochai: SO-chai, the ai like the start of hair, but short. Soch: rhymes, roughly, with coach, softened. Together, sochai soch: the same root twice, back and forth. Na hovaee: na, no; ho-VA-ee. Je sochee: jay SO-chee. Lakh vaar: lakh is a hundred thousand, the lakh you hear in Indian numbers; vaar is times. The meaning peeks through: soch is thinking, and lakh vaar is a hundred thousand times. The full meaning comes tomorrow. Today, the sound. Sochai, soch, sochee: three forms of one word in one short line. It sounds like what it describes, a mind going round and round, and it lands on lakh vaar, a number as tired as a mind at two in the morning. The rest of the pauri keeps the build. The next line begins chupai chup na hovaee: the same doubling, this time with chup, silence. Then a line about hunger with its own doubling, bhukhiaa bhukh, and then one about cleverness. Then the pauri stops and asks a question: kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai? Yesterday's word hides inside it: sach, in sachiaaraa, the one who is true. The last line gives the answer, with a word for tomorrow.
screen: `PAURI — A STEP ON A LADDER.` · `SOCHAI SOCH NA HOVAEE.` · `THE LINE LOOPS LIKE A MIND.` · `KIV SACHIAARAA HOEEAI?` · then, large: `PAURI ONE.`

segments.voice: Walk the line the way a mind walks a room: on one out-breath, sochai soch na hovaee; on the next, je sochee lakh vaar. Three times, slower each time, feeling the loop of soch, soch, sochee. Then let it go and sit; if your mind starts its own laps, just notice it pacing and let the breath be slower than the thoughts, and if you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

164.title: Pauri 1, meaning: the wall of falsehood
164.hook: thinking a hundred thousand times cannot reach Him; the wall of falsehood falls by walking in His order (Japji 1)
164.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the first pauri every morning in Japji; hukam is central to Sikh teaching, and the daily hukamnama read from the Guru Granth Sahib is received as the order for that day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of the first pauri and its question, kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai. Your line was sochai soch.

Four familiar tricks for getting closer to whatever matters most. Think harder: run it through your head again. Go quiet: a retreat, the phone in a drawer. Get more: the next purchase, the next raise will settle it. Get cleverer: one more book, one more podcast. Guru Nanak's first pauri takes tricks like these one at a time and gently closes each door. Then it opens a different one.
screen: `THINK HARDER. GO QUIET.` → `GET MORE. GET CLEVERER.` → `FOUR DOORS, GENTLY CLOSED.`

segments.voice: Here's the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. By thinking, He can't be reached, though you think a hundred thousand times. By keeping silent, you don't become silent inside, though you sit absorbed without end. The hunger of the hungry isn't satisfied, even by heaping up the goods of all the worlds. You may have a hundred thousand clevernesses, and not one goes with you. Thought, silence, having, cleverness: none of them is wicked. They just can't get you there. Some readers hear the first line as ritual cleansing instead: washing a hundred thousand times won't make the mind clean. Either way, effort alone falls short. Then the question. Kiv sachiaaraa hoeeai, kiv koorhai tutai paal? How do we become true? How is the wall of falsehood torn down? Paal is a wall or a bank, the kind that walls off a field; Macauliffe renders it as a veil. Koorh is the false, the fake. So a wall of falsehood stands between us and the true. And the answer: hukam rajaaee chalnaa, Naanak likhiaa naal. Walk in the hukam of the One whose will it is, written, says Nanak, along with us. Hukam runs all through Sikh life. It means an order, a command, the way a ruler's word goes out. In Japji it's bigger: the order of things, the will running through everything, the way the world actually is. You met a daily piece of it in camp three, the hukamnama. In the pauri, the wall doesn't come down by out-thinking it. It comes down by walking in step.
screen: `FOUR DOORS THAT DON'T OPEN.` · `KOORH — THE WALL OF FALSEHOOD.` · `HUKAM — THE ORDER, THE WILL.` · `WALK IN STEP WITH IT.` · then, large: `HUKAM.`

segments.voice: Pick one thing you've been turning over, a decision, a conversation, a worry, and instead of thinking about it again, set it down in front of you like a bag you've carried too far. Feel your feet on the floor and the breath going in and out on its own; in the pauri's language, that breath is already walking in the order, without a single thought. If you pray, you can let Waheguru carry the bag for a while.
Hukam. The order, the will running through everything. Japji's first pauri says the wall of falsehood falls by walking in it.
Your line: walk in the order. Four doors closed, and one door opened. Until tomorrow.

165.title: Pauri 2, sound: hukmee hovan
165.hook: hukmee hovan aakaar, hukam na kahiaa jaaee
165.tomorrow: Pauri 2, meaning: all within the order
165.howItsDone: The second pauri of Japji, with its repeated hukmee, is recited each morning; many Sikhs know its rhythm by heart before they study its meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hukam, the order running through everything, and the wall of falsehood. Your line was walk in the order.

Some songs hook you with their first word, because they keep coming back to it. By the second verse you're singing along before you know the rest. Kids' songs do it. Protest chants do it. The second pauri of Japji does it too. Yesterday's last word, hukam, becomes today's first, and then it comes back in every line that follows, like a drum you can't stop hearing.
screen: `A CHORUS THAT STARTS THE SAME.` → `YESTERDAY'S LAST WORD.` → `TODAY'S FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: The opening line: hukmee hovan aakaar, hukam na kahiaa jaaee. Sound it. Hukmee: HUK-mee, hukam with an ending that means by, or through: by the order. Hovan: HO-van, they come to be. Aakaar: aa-KAAR, forms, shapes. Then the second half. Hukam: the plain word again. Na kahiaa jaaee: na, not; KAH-i-aa, said; JAA-ee, can be. You can already feel it: by the order, forms come to be; the order itself can't be said. The full meaning comes tomorrow. Today, the build. The same word comes back in both halves of the next lines. Hukmee hovan jeea, hukam milai vadiaaee: by the order, living beings; by the order, greatness. Hukmee utam neech, hukam likh dukh sukh paaeeah: by the order, high and low; by the written order, sorrow and joy. A drumbeat: hukmee, hukam, hukmee, hukam. Then the pauri gathers everything up in one line with a lovely turn in its sound: hukmai andar sabh ko, baahar hukam na koe. Everyone is inside the order; outside the order, no one. Hear how andar, inside, and baahar, outside, answer each other. And the last line brings in a word you met in camp three, with seva and ego: haumai. What the pauri says about it waits for tomorrow.
screen: `HUKMEE — BY THE ORDER.` · `HUKMEE HOVAN AAKAAR.` · `THE SAME WORD IN EVERY LINE.` · `ANDAR AND BAAHAR — IN AND OUT.` · then, large: `PAURI TWO.`

segments.voice: Say the first line slowly, out loud if you can: hukmee hovan aakaar, hukam na kahiaa jaaee, three times, slower, then softer. Then, on each out-breath, just the drumbeat, hukmee, until it goes quiet and you're sitting with what your body does on its own: the heart, the breath, the small sounds. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.

166.title: Pauri 2, meaning: all within the order
166.hook: all forms, high and low, joy and pain, come by the order; whoever understands it no longer says I, I (Japji 2)
166.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the second pauri each morning; haumai, ego, is named in the Guru Granth Sahib as a deep obstacle, and seva, simran and sangat are the everyday ways of thinning it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the drumbeat of pauri two: hukmee, by the order. Your line was hukmee.

I got stuck in traffic. I had the worst meeting. I can't believe they said that to me. I, I, I. Nothing wrong with it; that's how stories work. But when a day goes badly, the I can get so big it fills the whole picture, and everything else, the traffic, the other people, the weather, becomes something that happened to me. Guru Nanak's second pauri ends by naming that I, and what makes it shrink.
screen: `I GOT STUCK. I CAN'T BELIEVE IT.` → `THE I FILLS THE PICTURE.` → `WHAT MAKES IT SHRINK?`

segments.voice: Here is the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. By the order, forms are made; the order can't be described. By the order, living beings come to be; by the order, some are given greatness. By the order some are high and some low; by the order, pain and joy are written. Some, by the order, are blessed; others, by the order, wander on and on. Everyone is within the order; no one is outside it. Then the last line: Nanak, whoever understands the order doesn't say I, I. The word there is haumai. Hau means I. Mai means me. I-me. You met it in camp three, as the ego that loves credit for its seva. Here it's bigger: the habit of standing outside everything, as if the world were happening to you alone. Sikh teaching names haumai as a deep trouble. Guru Angad, in a salok later in the Granth, calls it, in paraphrase, a long, deep illness, and then says the cure is inside it too. That's the hope the pauri holds out. If everything, high and low, joy and pain, is within the order, then no one stands outside it keeping score; each person is in it, with everyone else. Read that way, the traffic, the meeting and the rude remark are within the order too. That doesn't mean everything is fine, or that nothing should change; Sikh teaching also asks for honest work and standing against injustice. It means, in the pauri's terms, that the I stops being the center of the map, and the constant I, I goes quiet.

167.title: Pauri 3, sound: gaavai ko taan

167.howItsDone: The third pauri of Japji is recited each morning; its repeated gaavai ko, someone sings, is often a favorite for learners because the rhythm is easy to catch.

segments.voice: Yesterday, haumai, the I that fills the picture. Your line was all within the order.

A crowded room, and everyone is singing, but not the same song. One sings about how strong someone is. Another about their generosity. Another about how far away they seem, another about how close. It could be chaos. Instead it sounds like a choir that has agreed on one thing: whoever they're singing about is worth singing about. That's the third pauri of Japji, and its first two words are the whole idea: someone sings.
screen: `A ROOM FULL OF SINGERS.` → `EVERYONE A DIFFERENT SONG.` → `SOMEONE SINGS.`

segments.voice: The opening line: gaavai ko taan, hovai kisai taan. Gaavai: GAA-vai, sings. Ko: short and round, someone. Gaavai ko: someone sings. Taan: a long aa, and the n at the end is made with the tongue curled back a little. It means power, strength. Hovai: HO-vai, if there is, if one has. Kisai: KI-sai, to anyone. Roughly: someone sings of the power, if anyone has the power to sing it. The meaning opens tomorrow. Today, the build. Gaavai ko starts line after line, the way hukmee did in pauri two. Gaavai ko daat jaanai neesaan: someone sings of the gifts. Gaavai ko gun vadiaaeeaa chaar: someone sings of the virtues and the greatness. Gaavai ko, gaavai ko, until the room is full. Some lines swing between opposites: someone sings that He seems far away; someone, that He's right here, face to face. Then the pauri lifts out of the list with a new sound: kathnaa kathee na aavai tot. Kathnaa, kathee: telling, told. There's no end to the telling. Millions and millions tell it, the pauri says, and it never runs out. The last line ends on a word worth listening for, the sound of someone free of every worry: veparvaahu. For now, just the rhythm: gaavai ko, someone sings, voices joining a chorus one by one.

segments.voice: Hum a low note for a breath or two, then put the words on it: gaavai ko taan, hovai kisai taan, and if a tune wants to come, let it; this pauri is about singing. Twice more, slower, then softer. Then stop and listen to the silence after, as if the room of singers has just gone quiet; if you pray, you can rest in Waheguru.
Taan. Power, strength: what someone sings of, gaavai ko taan, line after line in this pauri.
Your line: gaavai ko. Someone sings, and then someone else joins. Day one hundred sixty-seven.

168.title: Pauri 3, meaning: the carefree one
168.hook: some sing His power, some His gifts; the Giver keeps giving though receivers tire, and He blossoms free of care (Japji 3)
168.howItsDone: Sikhs recite the third pauri each morning in Japji; its closing picture of the carefree Giver is often quoted in talks on gratitude and on giving without counting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of pauri three: gaavai ko taan, someone sings of strength. Your line was gaavai ko.

A grandmother at a family dinner keeps putting food on your plate. You say you're full. She adds another roti. You say really, I'm done. She's already bringing dessert. In the end you're the one who gives up; she never does. And she seems happy the whole time, not anxious, not keeping count. Guru Nanak's third pauri ends with a picture a little like that, only vast: a Giver who never tires, and receivers who do.
screen: `ANOTHER ROTI ON YOUR PLATE.` → `YOU GIVE UP FIRST.` → `A GIVER WHO NEVER TIRES.`

segments.voice: Here is the pauri in plain words, following Macauliffe. Some sing of His power, if they have the power. Some sing of His gifts, and know them as His sign. Some sing of His virtues, His greatness and His deeds. Some sing of knowledge gained through hard study. Some sing that He shapes the body and then turns it back to dust; some, that He takes life away and gives it again. Some, that He seems far away; some, that He watches face to face, always present. Millions upon millions tell it, and the telling never runs out. Then the turn. Dedaa de, laide thak paahi: the Giver keeps giving; the receivers grow tired of receiving. Through age after age, they go on eating. By His order, the One who orders sets the path. And the last line: Nanak, He blossoms, free of care. The word is veparvaahu. Parvaah is worry, concern; ve means without. Carefree. Not careless, as in not caring: the opposite of anxious. The Giver doesn't give out of need, or to be thanked, or while keeping count. In the pauri's picture, giving is simply what the Giver is. And vigsai, blossoms, is a flower word: opening, delighted. Notice what the pauri does with all those singers from yesterday. It doesn't pick a winner. Power, gifts, far, near: all sing of the same Giver, and none finishes. Some readers find relief in that: no singer has to get the song exactly right, and in the pauri the gifts keep coming anyway.
screen: `SOME SING POWER, SOME SING GIFTS.` · `NO END TO THE TELLING.` · `THE GIVER GIVES, RECEIVERS TIRE.` · `VEPARVAAHU — FREE OF CARE.` · then, large: `THE GIVER NEVER TIRES.`

segments.voice: Count three gifts from today, small and ordinary: the first sip of something warm, a text from someone, the breath you take without trying. Name each one quietly, without hurrying, and notice that you didn't make most of them; they arrived. If you pray, you can thank the Giver in a word, Waheguru; if you don't, just let yourself feel given to.
Veparvaahu. Free of care: the Giver keeps giving though some sing His power, some His gifts, and there's no end to the telling.
Your line: the giver never tires. The week behind you: sach, sochai soch, hukam, hukmee, haumai and gaavai ko. That's the week.
